Somnolent

/SOM-nuh-luhnt/ - the stress falls on SOM · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Somnolent means sleepy, drowsy.

The warm milk and the third bedtime story left Zoe somnolent at last, her questions arriving slower and slower.

Worked Example

The hammock, the cicadas, and the after-lunch sun made Theo somnolent within minutes; the paperback slid to the grass with his thumb still marking the page.

Somnolent is the precise word for the slide toward sleep—heavier than 'tired,' gentler than 'asleep.' Tired bodies ache; somnolent ones drift, eyelids losing the argument a little at a time.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

drowsy: Drowsy is the everyday word for the drift toward sleep—what you say in pajamas. Somnolent is the identical state in formal dress: a writer picks somnolent when the slide toward sleep should be felt in the prose. The difference is register, not meaning.

soporific: Soporific describes whatever causes the sleepiness, not the person feeling it: a soporific lecture, the soporific drone of rain. The listener it works on becomes somnolent. If the word answers 'what put you under?', it is soporific; if it answers 'how did you feel?', it is somnolent.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

alert: fully awake and tracking everything

wakeful: unable or unwilling to drift off

Where it sits · how close to losing consciousness — sleepy → somnolent → comatose

sleepy vs. somnolent: Sleepy is the first, mildest tug toward bed—a sleepy child still negotiates for one more story, while somnolent means the slide toward sleep has truly begun.

comatose vs. somnolent: Comatose goes far beyond sleepy or somnolent—it means unconscious outright, past being roused at all, while somnolent still hovers on sleep's doorstep.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — somn

Root — somn: sleep (Latin somnus)

Suffix — -olent

Suffix — -olent: full of, inclined to

Put it together

Put it together: Somn- (sleep, from Latin somnus) + -olent (full of, as in 'abounding in') = full of sleep. Somnus was Rome's god of sleep; his name still works the night shift in somnolent, insomnia, and the sleepwalker's somnambulism.

Use the root in a new word: insomnia

Use the root in a new word: insomnia: Flip the root with in- ('without') and you get insomnia—the long, lamp-lit misery of nights without sleep.

Word Choice

formal / literary

Somnolent is the dressed-up word for sleepy—use it when you want the drift toward sleep to be felt in the prose. Its unit-mates languid (weak and slow) and torpid (shut down, dormant) describe low energy without the pull toward sleep; somnolent is specifically the closing eyelid. For plain speech, drowsy does the same work in pajamas.
